chapter.title: Both Ways in One Process
chapter.para: The two directions are one bridge: a .NET application that runs Rexx code gives it .NET objects, which the Rexx code uses as NetObjects; a Rexx program that uses .NET gives it Rexx objects, which .NET code uses as RexxObjects. Each object comes back to its own side as itself, and calls nest on any thread.

section.title: .NET Objects in a Host's Rexx Code
section.para: A .NET object given to Rexx code (an argument of Run, a value in Local, the result of a command handler or a function) is a NetObject there, by reference, and the Rexx code uses it as in any Rexx program, &net; included. net.cls is loaded the first time a .NET object goes to Rexx; RequireNet loads it before, so that the code can use &net; without requiring it. &net; is in .environment: every instance of the process sees it.

.NET code that Rexx calls (a static method of the application, a handler) reaches the interpreter that called it through RexxInterpreter.Current, and its calls run nested on the same thread. A RexxObject parameter takes a Rexx object as itself (an Array too: then the overload that takes it wins over a copy).

example.title: Both ways in one process

section.title: Guest Mode
section.para: When ooRexx is the host (a program started by rexx that uses &net;), .NET code that the Rexx code calls gets a RexxInterpreter for the instance through RexxInterpreter.Current; its IsGuest is &true;, and Dispose does nothing on it. A .NET assembly of your own, loaded with .net~load, can so run Rexx code, send messages to the Rexx objects it is given, and throw exceptions that Rexx sees as 98.900. Application functions and value selectors need an instance made by Create.

section.title: Errors Across Both Directions
section.para: A .NET exception thrown by .NET code that Rexx called is a 98.900 in that Rexx code; if the Rexx code lets it out to the .NET code that ran it, that code gets a RexxException whose InnerException is the exception that was thrown, the very object. A RexxException thrown by .NET code that Rexx called (because Rexx code that it ran failed), through any chain of inner exceptions, is raised in the calling Rexx code as the original condition, with its code and message: the Rexx programmer gets their own error and line.

section.title: The NuGet Package
section.para: The package Rexx.Net holds lib/net8.0/Rexx.Net.dll and the native library rexxnet for Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (Apple silicon), in runtimes/rid/native/. The assembly carries net.cls and CLR.CLS inside it: when an instance is created (RexxOptions.Net, by default), they are loaded under their names, once per process, so that ::requires "net.cls" needs no file and uses the copy that matches the assembly; and rexxnet is registered with ooRexx, so net.cls's ::requires "rexxnet" LIBRARY needs no library path. The names are compared exactly: ::requires "net.cls" and ::requires CLR.CLS match, while ::requires NET.CLS (unquoted, so uppercased) looks for a file.

rexxnet is looked for as the application's own native library (the package's, through the application's deps.json), then in the directory that the environment variable REXXNET_DIR names, then next to Rexx.Net.dll. Without it, everything works but &net; in the Rexx code, and a .NET object going to Rexx says why. A Rexx program run by rexx (guest mode) uses the net.cls and rexxnet it finds on disk, as any package.

PowerShell 7.4 or later runs on .NET 8 or later and loads the assembly: Add-Type -Path Rexx.Net.dll (the project's samples/powershell/hello.ps1). Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs on .NET Framework, and cannot. A Rexx string is a RexxString there too, which PowerShell's + does not turn into a string: .ToString().
